newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Gulf War payout due in August if oil deal extended.
newsitem.headline: Gulf War payout due in August if oil deal extended.

text.p: Some 220,000 Gulf War victims are due to be paid $557 million in August if the current oil-for-food deal with Iraq is extended, U.N. sources said on Thursday.

But if the Security Council votes not to renew the six-month deal, which expires in June, the U.N. Compensation Commission will lack sufficient funds to pay each claimant in this round his or her $2,500 share, they added.
The Geneva-based body was set up by the Security Council in 1991 to compensate losses directly caused by Iraq's invasion of Kwuait in August 1990 and seven-month occupation of the emirate.

The fund, which receives 30 per cent of the revenue from the limited sale of Iraqi crude oil, last month paid $144 million to 57,636 claimants who proved they had been forced to leave Kuwait or Iraq, or had lost up to $100,000 in property.

It was the first major payout by the Commission, until then largely funded by donations and seized Iraqi assets. Previously it had paid $13.4 million to 3,966 people who proved death of a close relative or serious injury to themselves.

Under the renewable pact, Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of crude over the six-month period in order to buy food and medicine for civilians suffering from economic sanctions. The Geneva fund's 30 per cent share is $100 million a month.
"The money continues to come in regularly," a U.N. source in Geneva told Reuters. The body had received a total of $396 million so far from the U.N. oil deal with Baghdad, he added.

"Unless resolution 986 is extended in June beyond the original six-month period, there will not be sufficient funds in the Compensation Fund to make the second instalment payments of $2,500 each to successful claimants in categories A and C."
He was referring to some 220,000 claimants in the categories of "forced departure" or those with losses of up to $100,000.
"August is the target date (for payment) if resolution 986 were extended," the U.N. source added.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, speaking to a news conference in Geneva two weeks ago, said he expected the Security Council to renew the deal when its expires. Member states would see the humanitarian need among Iraqis and take into account Baghdad's obligations to pay Gulf War reparations.
Diplomats in New York also expect the Security Council to renew the pact for six more months at current oil sale limits.
The U.N. compensation body -- the largest reparations scheme ever -- has received claims against Iraq from individuals, corporations and governments valued at more than $220 billion.
Its Governing Council, composed of the same member states as the U.N. Security Council, was due to meet on April 28.

But as there was no report to consider from any of its panels of neutral arbitrators who evaluate claims and recommend awards, the meeting has been cancelled, according to U.N. officials. The Governing Council next meets from June 23-24.
